Support Vector Machine (SVM)
A model that says pass or fail for a new student, using the best dividing line between past passed and failed students.

The decision boundary
Students on one side are predicted to pass, on the other to fail.
The street
The empty band around the line. Its width is the margin: 2.46 here.
Support vectors
The students touching the street edges: 3 of the 12.
Maximum-margin classifier = support vector machine
4
A wide street survives new data
Narrow street

street 0.24 wide · average mistakes: 0.42
Widest street

street 2.46 wide · average mistakes: 0.06
Faded markers: the training students. Outlined markers: the same students measured again with a little noise (average over 3000 re-measurements).
5
Only the support vectors matter
Remove a student far away
Line unchanged
w = (0.73, 0.36) width 2.46
Move a support vector
The line moves
w = (1.07, 0.80) width 1.50
Dashed grey line: the original street’s centre.
Unlike other methods
Linear regression and k-means use every data point in their calculation. An SVM ends up depending on just the support vectors.
A caveat
The other students still matter in one way: they must stay outside the street. If one moved inside it, that student would become a support vector and the line would change. “Matter” here means “decide where the line sits”.

2k ÷ √(a₁² + a₂²)
= 2k ÷ √((k·w₁)² + (k·w₂)²)

= 2k ÷ √(k²·(w₁² + w₂²))
k² is a common factor

the root of k² is k
= 2k ÷ (k·√(w₁² + w₂²))
the k’s cancel
= 2 ÷ ‖w‖
